notes.meaning: The Lord personally called Bezalel from the tribe of Judah to lead the work on the tabernacle. God chose him by name so that no one would argue or feel jealous about who was placed in charge. When God gives his people an important assignment, he provides the right person to lead it.

God filled Bezalel with the Holy Spirit, giving him extraordinary wisdom, understanding, and practical skill. This is one of the earliest times in the Bible where the Spirit fills someone for a task beyond normal human ability. It shows that artistic and building skills used for God are honored and guided by his Spirit, just like preaching or leading.

God gave Bezalel the talent to design beautiful items in gold, silver, and bronze, as well as the skill to cut gems and carve wood. The Israelites had worked as slaves making bricks in Egypt, so God gave them special ability to handle fine and costly materials. Every gift needed to make the sacred tent beautiful came directly from God.

God selected Oholiab from the tribe of Dan to assist Bezalel, and he gave wisdom to a whole team of artisans to finish the work. Pairing a leader from Judah with an assistant from the less prominent tribe of Dan showed that God values people from every background. God calls believers to work together, combining different talents to serve him.

The Lord listed the sacred tent and its main furnishings that the workers were to build. These included the ark of the Testimony, the mercy seat where God met his people, the showbread table, the pure gold lampstand, and both altars. Naming each piece made sure that every item in God's dwelling place was built according to the exact plan he revealed.

The craftsmen were also directed to make the special clothing for the priests, the holy anointing oil, and the sweet-smelling incense. Everything had to be prepared strictly according to the commands the Lord had given to Moses. God sets the terms for how he is approached, and true worship follows his exact instructions.

The Lord commanded the Israelites to keep his Sabbaths as a visible sign of the special bond between them. Resting on the seventh day reminded them that the Lord was the one who made them holy, meaning set apart for his service. Even the urgent and sacred work of building the tabernacle was not allowed to interrupt God's day of rest.

The Sabbath was holy, and anyone who treated it like an ordinary workday faced the death penalty and separation from the community. Disregarding the day of rest was a direct rebellion against God's covenant relationship with his people. This strict warning taught Israel that life with God requires full obedience to his commands.

The people were permitted to do their regular work during six days, but the seventh day was set aside for complete rest dedicated to the Lord. Working on this day brought the sentence of death. Putting down tools each week showed that they trusted God to provide for their needs rather than relying only on their own effort.

Israel was commanded to keep the Sabbath through every generation as a lasting covenant sign. The weekly rest pointed back to the creation of the world, when the Lord made everything in six days and rested on the seventh. By taking this holy rest, God's people refreshed their bodies and minds while following the example of their Creator.

differ.view: The moral duty to set apart one day in seven for holy rest continues for Christians as a lasting command.
The seventh-day Sabbath covenant was a temporary shadow given specifically to Israel that ended with the coming of Christ.

notes.meaning: When the Lord finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, he gave him two stone tablets containing the Ten Commandments. These laws were inscribed by the finger of God, which means they were written directly by God's own power. Carving the commandments into durable stone showed that his covenant law was solid and permanent.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Because ancient covenants usually gave a written copy to each party, the two stone tablets may have been two identical copies of the agreement—one for God and one for Israel—rather than the commandments split across two stones.
